payload.name: Lumos

media.alt: Luminous magic illuminating a dark fantasy setting
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: Illuminates dark spaces. Nox is its wand-extinguishing counterspell.
payload.effect: Produces a light at the wand tip that remains useful for exploring dark places until extinguished with Nox.

breakdown.label: Lumos
breakdown.meaning: The complete incantation; the syllables above are a reading aid, not separate translated words.

payload.etymology: The official etymology guide suggests a connection to the Latin lumen, meaning light. It presents this origin as a possibility.
payload.continuity: Harry Potter novels; also depicted in the film adaptations
payload.definition: Creates light at the tip of a wand.
payload.pronunciationNote: An English reader aid, rather than an official phonetic transcription. Accents can vary across performances.

payload.name: Fus Ro Dah

media.alt: An expanding wave of force sweeping across a rugged landscape
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: Its full three-word form can send opponents airborne. Strength and effects depend on the game context.
payload.effect: A forceful vocal blast pushes enemies away; the complete three-word shout can launch them into the air.

breakdown.label: Fus
breakdown.meaning: The first word of the three-word shout.

breakdown.label: Ro
breakdown.meaning: The second word of the three-word shout.

breakdown.label: Dah
breakdown.meaning: The final word of the three-word shout.

payload.etymology: Bethesda describes the Dragon language as drawing on several Germanic languages, especially Old English. This is language inspiration; an individual word-origin analysis is not confirmed here.
payload.continuity: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
payload.definition: A Dragon Shout that pushes opponents away with powerful force.
payload.pronunciationNote: An approximate English reader aid. Bethesda identifies each word as a single syllable; the in-game voice is the performance reference.

payload.name: Brisingr

media.alt: Swirling flames glowing against a dark fantasy backdrop
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: A fire-related word of power. A word’s translation alone does not describe every possible magical effect.
payload.effect: Names fire in the Ancient Language and supplies a fire-related word for magic; the intended result depends on how it is used.

breakdown.label: Brisingr
breakdown.meaning: Fire — the complete Ancient Language word.

payload.etymology: Paolini explains that he found brisingr, meaning fire, in an Old Norse word-origin reference and used it as inspiration for the Ancient Language.
payload.continuity: Inheritance Cycle novels; Ancient Language word entry
payload.definition: The Ancient Language word for fire, used in the series’ magic.
payload.pronunciationNote: Paolini’s official website supplies this pronunciation for the sword bearing the same word, and provides an audio pronunciation guide.

payload.name: Alohomora

media.alt: Magical light unlocking an ornate door
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: Hermione uses it on the forbidden third-floor corridor door in the first book.
payload.effect: Unlocks a locked door, allowing the caster to open it; the cited example is Hermione’s escape into the forbidden third-floor corridor.

sources.label: Harry Potter · Philosopher’s Stone Spell Guide

breakdown.label: Alohomora
breakdown.meaning: The complete incantation; no component translations are asserted here.

payload.etymology: An origin for this incantation has not been confirmed by the primary references included in this entry.
payload.continuity: Harry Potter novels; the cited scene is from Philosopher’s Stone
payload.definition: An unlocking charm used to open locked doors.
payload.sourceTitle: Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone
payload.pronunciationNote: An English reader aid. The linked official story guide confirms the spell and its use, but does not supply this phonetic spelling.

payload.name: Wingardium Leviosa

media.alt: A feather suspended in the air by levitation magic
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: Associated with the swish-and-flick wand movement and careful pronunciation.
payload.effect: Raises an object into the air. Ron uses the charm on a mountain troll’s club after learning it in Professor Flitwick’s class.

sources.label: Harry Potter · Philosopher’s Stone Spell Guide

breakdown.label: Leviosa
breakdown.meaning: Second word; the official guide highlights its pronunciation.

payload.etymology: The supplied official reference explains the charm’s use, but does not establish a complete linguistic derivation.
payload.continuity: Harry Potter novels; the cited lesson is from Philosopher’s Stone
payload.definition: Makes an object levitate.
payload.pronunciationNote: An English reader aid. The official guide emphasizes the Levi-o-sa pronunciation; the full respelling here is not an official transcription.

payload.name: Expelliarmus

media.alt: A wand flying away amid a burst of disarming magic
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: A practical disarming charm associated with Harry’s duelling.
payload.effect: Makes a target release a held object, commonly a wand, and gives a duellist a way to disarm an opponent.

breakdown.label: Expelliarmus
breakdown.meaning: The official explanation gives the combined meaning “drive out a weapon”; no exact morpheme boundary is claimed here.

payload.etymology: The official guide describes a combination of Latin with the approximate sense of driving out a weapon.
payload.continuity: Harry Potter novels; Harry learns it during the Chamber of Secrets Duelling Club
payload.definition: Forces an opponent to release what they are holding, often a wand.
payload.pronunciationNote: An English reader aid rather than an official phonetic transcription. Performances may vary.

payload.name: Expecto Patronum

media.alt: A luminous animal guardian casting protective light through mist
media.caption: Original illustration inspired by the spell’s fictional effect

payload.usage: An advanced defensive charm; Patronuses can also carry messages in the stories.
payload.effect: Creates a protective positive force against Dementors. A fully formed Patronus takes an animal shape, and some casters use Patronuses to deliver messages.

sources.label: Harry Potter · What Is a Patronus?

breakdown.label: Expecto
breakdown.meaning: I expect or await, in the official guide’s approximate Latin translation.

breakdown.label: Patronum
breakdown.meaning: A guardian or protector, in the official guide’s approximate Latin translation.

payload.etymology: The official etymology guide connects the Latin phrase with expecting or awaiting a guardian; patronus carries the sense of a protector.
payload.continuity: Harry Potter novels; first taught to Harry in Prisoner of Azkaban
payload.definition: Conjures a protective Patronus to oppose Dementors.
payload.sourceTitle: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
payload.pronunciationNote: An English reader aid. The source confirms the written incantation, but does not supply this phonetic transcription.
